item.title: Why a common cold can trigger an asthma flare: A single protein may fuel two kinds of inflammation
item.description:

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on a medical condition with clear, technical detail and useful vocabulary.

Why a common cold can trigger an asthma flare: A single protein may fuel two kinds of inflammation

A common cold can quickly trigger an asthma episode, with respiratory viruses such as rhinovirus being among the most common culprits. During these viral flare-ups, levels of G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) rise in the body. This growth factor protein regulates the production, release and survival of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell that helps fight infections. A recent study investigated how the single protein G-CSF acts as a master driver of severe lung inflammation during viral asthma flare-ups and whether blocking it could lead to a powerful new treatment.

The researchers tracked daily respiratory symptoms, lung capacity and G-CSF levels in 28 asthma patients and 11 healthy control participants, then experimentally inoculated them with rhinovirus A16, the common cold virus, as the disease progressed.

When infected with the common cold virus, rhinovirus, asthma patients experienced a sharp surge in G-CSF levels, an increase that was absent in healthy individuals. This rise in G-CSF was accompanied by stronger inflammatory responses and higher amounts of the virus. Across the human cohort, greater G-CSF gene activity was also associated with more severe lower-airway symptoms, although it did not correspond to larger declines in lung function.

These findings were published in Science Translational Medicine.

Double whammy of inflammation

Sudden asthma flare-ups account for most asthma-related hospitalizations and are most commonly triggered by respiratory viruses such as rhinovirus. Allergic asthma is traditionally viewed as a type 2 inflammatory disease driven by eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. However, viral infections complicate this picture, triggering both type 2 and neutrophilic inflammation in the lungs at the same time.

The standard treatment for acute flare-ups relies heavily on oral corticosteroids. While the steroids effectively suppress type 2 allergic inflammation, the same cannot be said about their effects on neutrophilic inflammation. This led scientists to investigate whether a single biological switch could be driving both inflammatory responses during viral infections.

They turned their attention to G-CSF, which is known to control the production and survival of neutrophils. Recent studies had also begun to hint that G-CSF could fuel type 2 allergic inflammation by acting on other immune cells, although the evidence was not yet strong enough to establish this role.

In search of what drives the flare-ups both ways, the team collected bronchial brushings and bronchoalveolar fluid at baseline and on day 4 post-infection, along with nasal lavage samples across days 0 to 10. For 14 days, they monitored daily lower and upper respiratory symptoms as well as lung function, G-CSF gene and protein levels, viral load, neutrophils and type 2 allergic cytokines. To examine the underlying cellular mechanisms, female mice were sensitized to an allergen to simulate allergic asthma and then infected intranasally with rhinovirus.

Protein holds the key

The experiments revealed that G-CSF does more than regulate neutrophils. It can also directly fuel type 2 allergic inflammation by activating allergic immune cells, including ILC2s, dendritic cells and CD4+ TH2 cells. This, in turn, boosts the production of allergic cytokines, along with eosinophils. They also found that giving recombinant G-CSF to allergic mice was enough on its own to trigger a full-blown asthma flare-up.

The next step was to see if blocking G-CSF could stop both inflammatory responses from spiraling out of control during a viral flare-up. The researchers found that mice treated with a G-CSF-blocking antibody had fewer neutrophils and allergic immune cells crowding their lungs and airways. The treatment also eased airway stiffness and breathing resistance in mice, while preventing tissue damage and excessive mucus buildup.

The findings make a case for blocking G-CSF to treat asthma attacks triggered by the cold virus. The researchers, however, noted one important limitation. In the mouse studies, G-CSF-blocking treatment was given just before virus exposure, whereas in real life, treatment would likely begin after an asthma attack has started. They suggest that future studies could test the treatment at this stage to make the findings more clinically relevant.

item.title: The hippocampus helps people infer new relationships from familiar patterns, experiments suggest
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains a cognitive process with clear language and useful context for learning.

The hippocampus helps people infer new relationships from familiar patterns, experiments suggest

When trying to understand a new situation or scenario, humans usually try to work out connections between the different elements involved. If they recognize a familiar pattern, they can use mental connections established from past experiences to guide their interpretation and decisions.

The ability to infer relationships in new situations based on overall patterns is referred to as structure-based inference. It can be very useful, as it helps people to adapt their world interpretations in changing and unfamiliar circumstances.

Researchers at the University of Oxford recently carried out a study aimed at better understanding how the brain supports structure-based inference. Their paper, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggests that a brain region called the hippocampus, which is central to the encoding and retrieval of memories, helps people to use previously learned relationships to make sense of new situations.

"Our study was motivated by two simple questions: how do we learn the underlying structure behind our experiences, and how do we use that knowledge to make inferences in new situations?" Deng Pan, first author of the paper, told Medical Xpress.

"In everyday life, we rarely learn everything from scratch. Instead, we recognize patterns across different experiences and use what we have learned before to understand something new. We wanted to understand how the human brain supports this ability, and particularly whether the hippocampus, a brain region important for learning and memory, plays a causal role in learning relational knowledge and using it to make inferences."

Assessing how people learn and infer relationships

To investigate the neural underpinnings of structure-based inference, Pan and his colleagues carried out a series of experiments in which participants played a game on a computer screen. The game they designed, called the Goalkeeper Game, required participants to learn the relationships between several players.

"The game allowed us to study how people recognize the 'structure' underlying these relationships and then use this knowledge to infer new ones," said Pan.

As 36 participants played the Goalkeeper Game on a computer, the researchers scanned their brains using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that tracks changes in blood oxygenation linked to brain activity. The team analyzed the collected scans to identify patterns representing the relationships between characters.

Subsequently, they also used computational models, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs), to investigate the processes supporting learning and inference.

"We combined several different approaches," explained Pan. "We used brain imaging to ask where this relational 'structure' is represented in the brain and found that the answer was the hippocampus. We built reinforcement learning models to understand participants' behavior, and RNNs to model the neural computations that might support this process."

In a follow-up experiment, the researchers noninvasively and temporarily modulated activity in the hippocampus of 20 participants before they started playing the game. They did this using a technique called transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), which sends ultrasound waves through the skull.

"This allowed us to directly test whether the hippocampus causally contributes to learning relationships and making new inferences," said Pan.

The team observed that during the experiment, participants were able to infer relationships between players that they had not directly experienced, using previously learned connections to fill gaps in what they knew. Moreover, stimulating the hippocampus appeared to disrupt this ability to infer relationships based on learned connections.

"Although the whole study is important, I think the key contribution is that we provided causal evidence for the role of the hippocampus in high-level cognition in healthy humans," said Pan. "We believe this is a major step forward in how we study hippocampal function in healthy humans. This has traditionally been difficult because it required studying patients with hippocampal damage, while conventional noninvasive stimulation cannot easily reach the hippocampus deep inside the brain."

The promise of TUS for studying flexible learning

Using TUS, Pan and his colleagues were able to temporarily alter activity in the hippocampus, assessing the effects of this on people's behavior. In addition to uncovering the role of the hippocampus in structure-based inference, their study thus highlights the potential of TUS for conducting neuroscience and psychology research.

"We hope TUS could be a game changer for bridging the gap between high-level cognition, such as learning, inference and decision-making, and its neural basis in healthy humans, especially when these processes involve deep brain regions such as the hippocampus," said Pan. "For future research, I would like to use TUS to study a broader range of high-level cognitive functions that interest me. Many of these, such as problem-solving, reasoning and planning, are difficult to study in animals."

Pan is currently planning more experiments that will rely on TUS to temporarily alter people's brain activity. He thinks that the technique could be particularly useful for examining functions that are supported by regions situated deep inside the brain, which have proved difficult to study noninvasively.

"In the longer term, I would like to better understand the mechanisms of TUS neuromodulation and explore how it could be developed into noninvasive treatments for disorders involving deep brain regions," added Pan. "For example, this could include targeting hippocampal circuits involved in memory or amygdala-related circuits involved in emotion in conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)."…

Why it is here: Focuses on a new initiative with clear reporting and useful information for mental health awareness.

New project to provide free mental health courses

Adults across Sussex will be able to access free mental health and recovery courses through a new county-wide project launching in 2027.

The Sussex Recovery College is offering courses covering mental health, wellbeing, recovery, personal growth and creativity from January.

It will bring together existing services across Brighton and Hove, East Sussex and West Sussex into a single programme.

Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust, one of the partners in the project, said research involving people already using the existing services showed hospital admissions fell in the 18 months after they registered to take part.

The research showed that in the 18 months, average hospital admissions fell by 34% and the number of days spent in hospital fell by 55%, the trust said.

A 50% reduction in admissions under the Mental Health Act was also reported, it added.

The trust is developing the county-wide service with Southdown, which is the project's voluntary sector partner.

Matt Gough, the charity's chief operating officer, said his organisation was bringing more than 10 years' experience of running the Brighton and Hove Recovery College to the project.

Courses that were offered in 2024-25 looked at specific health conditions and included creative activities such as writing, music and singing.

"We've seen first-hand the difference recovery education can make, helping people build confidence, develop new skills, connect with others and find ways to support their mental health and wellbeing," he said.

Courses are co-produced and delivered by people with lived experience, NHS clinicians, peer trainers and specialists.

Students will be able to attend face-to-face local courses or take part online.

Dr Oliver Dale, chief medical officer at the trust, said: "Recovery colleges play an important role in supporting people's mental health, wellbeing and recovery."

He said the new service would create greater opportunities for people to learn, connect and support their recovery journey.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

item.title: Swinney insists Scotland's NHS is safe despite hospital scandal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Reports on a health scandal with clear information, though not as in-depth as the top pick.

Swinney insists Scotland's NHS is safe despite hospital scandal

The first minister has insisted that Scotland's NHS is "fundamentally safe" despite concerns raised about care at NHS Grampian.

The health board has continued to face scrutiny following the publication of a leaked report that revealed 19 avoidable deaths among 45 patients in liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI).

Last week, the Scottish government announced an independent review into concerns around hepatobiliary (HPB) surgery at the health board.

John Swinney acknowledged that mistakes can occur but insisted patients should still attend appointments, procedures and surgeries.

Speaking at an anti-racism rally for St Andrew's Day in Glasgow, Swinney said: "We have a fundamentally safe National Health Service in Scotland that operates to the highest level of quality.

"There are issues that go wrong, I accept there are some issues that go wrong.

"But fundamentally we have a safe, strong and effective National Health Service, and I would encourage the public to participate in that service."

When asked about claims the Scottish government was aware of the decision not to publish the 2022 report, Swinney said the upcoming review would answer any questions.

He said: "I want to make sure there is total transparency about all of these issues, that we understand what went on, what was the sequence of events, what judgments were made, and that there can be lessons learnt from all of that."

The first minister said the government had to "satisfy members of the public with our answers".

"But this is in one isolated area of surgery, in NHS Grampian," he added.

"Every day, there are thousands and thousands and thousands and thousands of procedures that are carried out in the National Health Service perfectly safely, perfectly effectively by high-quality professionals, clinicians and members of staff and that should give members the public confidence."

Martin McKay, from Unison's Grampian health branch, said staff had faced abuse at hospitals since concerns about NHS Grampian were raised earlier this month.

"Staff are being abused, being called killers, asked if they're bringing their butcher's knives to work with them," he told BBC Scotland News. "And that's just horrendous.

"People need to take a step back and have a serious look at themselves.

"Abusing staff who are working hard in difficult circumstances to deliver care on a daily basis is just unacceptable."

He added: "People will have legitimate issues to raise and that's entirely their choice, but to suggest that all staff are complicit in this is just preposterous and counterproductive to staff trying to deliver healthcare."

'Major deficiencies'

NHS Grampian has been at the centre of controversy since a report from the health watchdog published two weeks ago highlighted "major deficiencies" in its leadership and culture.

Healthcare Improvement Scotland's medical director Dr Simon Watson described the report as "the most serious review" it had ever written, calling the findings "unprecedented".

Dr Mohammed Habib, a consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), leaked the 2022 report the following week.

He called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide probe.

An oversight team was appointed for NHS Grampian, and Health Secretary Angela Constance announced an independent review of the health board last week.

She said it would be carried out by experts from outside Scotland and be "100% transparent".

A number of patients have come forward to raise concerns about their treatment.

One woman said she lay awake on an operating table during knee replacement surgery listening to surgeons argue as they struggled to control her bleeding.

While another patient said he felt mistakes were made after he went into cardiac arrest during a liver operation.

On Thursday, Scotland's chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith, who had faced questions over his role, resigned on mental health grounds.

The chairwoman of the BMA in Scotland said trust had been damaged across the NHS by the revelations and this should be a watershed moment for healthcare in Scotland.

Separately, the health board apologised on Friday after confidential papers containing sensitive medical and personal details of 22 patients were found discarded on a street near the ARI.

A passer-by found the documents near a bin on Raeden Park Road, near Foresterhill Health Campus, the day before.
